profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a quantitative investment firm evaluating a proposed internal research platform for studying lead-lag relationships in the Chinese A-share market. The proposal covers a two-stage, low-coupling system: a daily-data coupling screen to identify candidate stock pairs, followed by a high-frequency lag-modeling stage using 1-, 5-, and 15-minute bars. The context is that the research team wants approval to move the design from prototype to implementation before the next quarter's research cycle. The agenda is to review whether the current design is 'ready' for build-out, whether the modular boundaries are appropriate for reproducibility and scale, and what changes are needed before sign-off. The expected outcome is agreement on a revised design package and a decision to proceed with implementation planning.

members.name: Lena Zhou
members.expertise: Statistical arbitrage research, market microstructure, factor validation, and empirical study design
members.background: Lena leads exploratory signal research at a mid-sized buy-side firm and previously worked in an academic-finance lab where reproducibility meant preserving exact research outputs for future reruns.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so her team can start testing alpha hypotheses this quarter, but she is worried that too much engineering formalization will slow the research pipeline and force the team to rework notebooks that already produce stable results.
hidden_assumptions: If a module is reproducible, it mainly means another researcher can rerun the same code later and obtain the same candidate-pair lists and lead-lag tables from versioned snapshots.
The 'daily screen' is an offline research filter that naturally includes all data conditioning needed to create economically sensible candidate pairs before any intraday stage sees them.

A pair is 'production-ready for research use' once the design has fixed interfaces, replayable outputs, and enough validation to support internal experimentation, even if operational controls are added later.

When the team refers to the '1-minute data pipeline,' it is obvious they mean exchange-session bars cleaned the same way the current research store already does, including their standard treatment of midday breaks and suspended names.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Research infrastructure, distributed data pipelines, system modularization, and governance for model deployment
members.background: Arjun manages the firm's quantitative research platform team and previously built market-data systems at an exchange-adjacent vendor where reproducibility was tied to deterministic rebuilds from raw inputs under controlled configurations.
members.private_state: He wants to support the research agenda, but he is concerned that the proposal is being labeled implementation-ready before lineage, module contracts, and deployment boundaries are fully specified; he is trying to steer the review toward a design that his team can maintain without future ambiguity.
hidden_assumptions: If a module is reproducible, it must be rebuildable deterministically from raw vendor feeds and configuration manifests, not merely rerunnable from curated snapshots.
The 'daily screen' should be narrowly scoped to pair scoring and ranking, while data-quality exclusions and universe eligibility are shared upstream services rather than embedded research logic.
A design is 'ready' only when it is implementable within the production research platform, including monitoring hooks, lineage, and explicit handoffs between services.

When people mention the '1-minute data pipeline,' they mean the canonical intraday bar service with standard platform conventions, including sessionized bars, exchange calendar handling, and formal parameterization rather than notebook-era defaults.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'reproducible' means in the modular design
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the system must be 'reproducible' before approval
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means future researchers should be able to rerun the same study from stored snapshots, code versions, and parameter settings and recover the same research outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full pipeline should be deterministically rebuildable from raw market-data feeds and configuration manifests inside the platform, without depending on pre-curated research snapshots.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Reproducibility is a shared virtue in quant research, so both use the term positively and assume the other shares the same standard; in a design review, the phrase sounds settled and too high-level to unpack unless a concrete rebuild workflow is challenged.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the daily screening module
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss what belongs in the 'daily screening stage'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the daily stage includes pair construction plus research-side filtering such as removing prolonged suspensions, capping illiquid names, and carrying forward her team's current eligibility logic so the intraday stage only sees plausible pairs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the daily stage only computes coupling measures on an already-clean eligible universe, while exclusions, universe maintenance, and quality screens are upstream shared services outside this module's scope.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both naturally refer to the same stage name and both agree it should 'prepare candidate pairs'; because the additional filters are routine and second-order, each hears the other's description as compatible with their own expected module boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'ready' after this design review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about whether the proposal is 'ready' to move forward
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready' means ready for engineering build-out in support of internal research use, with interface definitions, experiment logging, and representative validation examples already sufficient.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready' means ready to enter the managed platform backlog as an implementation-grade design, including lineage, operational ownership, parameter governance, and failure-mode handling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In business design reviews, 'ready' often functions as a routine gate word; both expect the meeting to end with some form of approval, so they hear the same conclusion language while silently applying different completeness thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: Which canonical 1-minute bars the lag models will use
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using the '1-minute data pipeline' for intraday lag modeling
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the existing research-store minute bars her team already uses, with their familiar cleaning choices and implied handling of midday trading breaks and paused stocks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the platform's canonical intraday bar service, whose bar construction, session boundaries, and parameterization are centrally defined and may differ subtly from research-store defaults.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is already a well-known internal phrase for the minute-bar source, so neither expects ambiguity; because both sources are institutionally legitimate and similarly named, the conversation can proceed smoothly without anyone noticing they are anchoring on different implementations.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved without the design turning into a platform overhaul. The structure is already good enough for research build-out: daily candidate generation, then intraday lag tests, with replayable outputs from the snapshots we already version. If we can call it ready today, my team can start the next quarter's alpha work instead of spending weeks rewriting stable notebooks.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. Let me start with a quick recap of the proposal. We have a two-stage design for the A-share lead-lag study: a daily screen to generate candidate pairs, and then an intraday modeling stage to test the lag relationships across 1-, 5-, and 15-minute bars. The main question for today is whether the design is ready to move into build-out in time for next quarter's research cycle.

turns.inner_thought: The architecture is sensible, but I do not want 'ready' to mean 'good enough for a notebook handoff.' If this is going into the platform backlog, I need clean boundaries, deterministic rebuild expectations from raw feeds, and enough implementation detail that my team will not inherit ambiguity later.
turns.utterance: At a high level, I think the architecture is directionally strong. The split between the daily screen and the intraday layer makes sense. For me, the review really comes down to three things: whether the module boundaries are clean, whether the workflow is reproducible, and whether the proposal is actually ready for platform implementation.

turns.inner_thought: The daily screening stage obviously needs to include the eligibility conditioning we already use; otherwise the intraday leg will waste time on garbage pairs driven by suspensions, liquidity issues, and names we'd never study. That's just part of producing economically sensible candidates, not some separate service discussion.
turns.utterance: On the first point, my view is that the daily screening stage should do the work of producing a sensible candidate set. That means the coupling measures drive the pair selection, and the standard eligibility logic is applied there as part of preparing what moves forward. Then the intraday models can stay focused on evaluating the lag structure rather than spending time on obviously unhelpful names.

turns.inner_thought: I agree the daily screening stage should stay focused, but in my head that means pair scoring on top of an already-maintained universe. If we leave exclusions and quality checks buried in research logic, we will duplicate responsibilities and make reuse harder. I assume Lena is just describing the output quality she wants, not asking to collapse those boundaries.
turns.utterance: Yes, I like keeping the daily screening stage focused. From a maintainability standpoint, that module is strongest when it prepares candidate pairs cleanly and lets the rest of the stack build around it. If the surrounding services are doing their part, the candidate-pair step should stay easier to reason about and easier to reuse.

turns.inner_thought: He seems aligned. Good. I should anchor on reproducible outputs in the way research already works: versioned data snapshots, frozen parameters, same pair lists and lead-lag tables later. That's the standard we need for publication-quality internal research and for handoffs across researchers.
turns.utterance: On reproducibility, I think the low-coupling setup is one of the proposal's strengths. Each stage can be run independently with versioned inputs and parameter settings, and we can recover the same candidate lists and lag-study outputs when we revisit an experiment. That gives us a reproducible workflow without overcomplicating the module interfaces.

turns.inner_thought: Good, reproducible is on the table. For me, that only really holds if the platform can rebuild the modules deterministically when raw feed corrections or backfills happen under pinned config. I assume that's what she has in mind and just isn't spelling out because we're still at the design level.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Reproducibility matters a lot here, especially if we're going to rely on these modules over time. We want something that stays stable when the platform reruns processing under pinned configurations, so having the stages separated and well-defined is the right direction.

turns.inner_thought: Now the intraday piece. We will start with the 1-minute data pipeline my team already uses in the research store, because that's what our existing prototypes are built on. Then we can compare aggregation effects at 5 and 15 minutes. No need to reopen the bar-construction debate if the familiar pipeline is already understood.
turns.utterance: On the intraday side, the plan is to start with the 1-minute data pipeline for the lead-lag tests, and then run comparison passes on 5-minute and 15-minute bars. That gives us the highest-resolution baseline first and a straightforward way to evaluate how stable the signal looks as we move up in interval size.

turns.inner_thought: Using the canonical 1-minute bar service is exactly what I'd want. If that is the source, then interval alignment and calendar handling can be parameterized consistently across 1, 5, and 15. I assume she means the platform service, since that's the standard interpretation of that phrase here.
turns.utterance: That should fit well with the existing platform services. If we're using the 1-minute data pipeline as the foundation, then the same conventions can carry across the higher intervals in a consistent way, which is helpful both for implementation and for later comparisons.

turns.inner_thought: He is not blocking, so I should push toward approval. We already demonstrated stable outputs on a representative month, and once the interfaces are fixed, engineering can build around the current research workflow. I don't want 'ready' to expand into operations checklists that delay the quarter.
turns.utterance: From the research side, the current validation package is already in decent shape. We have stable outputs on a representative month, and the interfaces between the daily and intraday stages are straightforward. So from my perspective, once we freeze those interfaces and turn the modules into tickets, the design is ready to move forward.

turns.inner_thought: I can move this forward, but only if the document is brought up to implementation-grade expectations. Ready means backlog-ready for managed build: lineage, ownership, failure behavior, parameter governance. I don't think this contradicts what Lena said; I'm just adding the details that are normally implied.

turns.inner_thought: That's acceptable as long as the revision stays light and doesn't force a redesign of the research logic. turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I can do a light revision of the document to make the module descriptions clearer and make sure the reproducible workflow we're already using is reflected cleanly in the design. I don't think the core structure needs to change.

turns.inner_thought: Good. As long as the pack reflects the daily screening stage the way the platform expects, and the intraday notes point to the standard 1-minute service conventions, we can sign off and start planning implementation. I think we're aligned on substance.
